title: "Spatial Structure and Determinants of Global Top Biomedical Scientists' Mobility from an Urban Network Perspective"
---

::: {.page-band .surface .paper-page}

<p class="paper-meta">Authors: Ran Wang (First author) · Status: Accepted · Journal: World Regional Studies</p>

## Research Summary

This accepted article examines how the education and employment moves of global top biomedical scientists are organised across cities. Using verified career histories for 500 scientists from 1970 to 2023, it constructs directed intercity mobility networks and relates mobility ties to city-level scientific and institutional conditions. The study distinguishes learning-stage and employment-stage mobility, showing that top-scientist movement is spatially selective, centered strongly on U.S. cities, and patterned differently across career stages.

## Abstract

<p class="abstract-text">As a knowledge- and capital-intensive field, biomedicine has become a central arena of global innovation competition. This study focuses on the world's top biomedical scientists and analyzes their mobility trajectories from an urban-network perspective. Using complex network analysis and Heckman two-stage regression, the paper examines factors associated with scientist mobility across career stages. The study finds that: ① the mobility of top biomedical scientists presents a network structure centered on the United States, with substantial cross-continent movement. In the learning stage, mobility is more unidirectional, concentrated, and unipolar, and top scientists tend to move to university-dense areas. In the working stage, mobility becomes more polycentric and networked, with scientists more likely to choose research institutions and industrial bases. ② Top-scientist mobility is highly selective. Migration is associated with scientific output, academic influence, interdisciplinary background, and related factors. Regions with dense research resources and strong scientific ecology attract top scientists, while institutional barriers and cultural differences constrain global scientific talent mobility.</p>
